rashi:a1.1: And the intercalated month of the year was thirty: there you have one full month. And last year we made both of them full, Marḥeshvan and Iyyar: there you have three full months beyond the regular order. Therefore, when three are made deficient now, against them, the moon stands in its place.
rashi:a1.2: Lamp of Israel: for you light up the eyes of the Sages.
gershom:a1.1: And last year we made both of them full: so two days were left over, and the day added in the intercalation was the third. This accords with Rav Huna, who said that we make eight full months.
gershom:a2.1: [Remove three of these nine deficient months against those three; therefore it stands in its place, and the moon was seen in its time.]
gershom:a3.1: Lamp of Israel, so it was: that is, you are the one who gives light [like a lamp] to Israel, for you knew how to work the matter out.
rashi:a2.1: Mishna. Twenty-one blasts and forty-eight blasts: these are explained in tractate Sukkah, in the chapter HeḤalil (Sukkah 53b).
tosafot:a2.1: (This belongs to the mishna.) No fewer than twenty-one blasts in the Temple each day: it is explained in Sukkah (53b): three for the opening of the gates, and nine for the daily morning offering, for the Levites would sing at the time of the libations, the song had three sections, and for each section they sounded a tekia, a terua and a tekia.
gershom:a4.1: [Rabbeinu Gershom here returns to lines of the mishna on 8b.] Mishna: The two loaves are eaten no sooner than the second day and no later than the third. How so? They are baked on the eve of Atzeret [Shavuot] and eaten on Atzeret, which is the second day; if the festival falls right after Shabbat, they are eaten on the third.
gershom:a5.1: The showbread is baked on Friday and eaten on the following Shabbat, on the ninth day. If a festival falls on Friday, it is eaten on the tenth; if the two days of Rosh HaShana [fall before Shabbat], it is eaten on the eleventh, since its baking overrides neither Shabbat nor a festival.
gershom:a6.1: A minor is not circumcised sooner than the eighth day: this is explained in tractate Shabbat, in the chapter Rabbi Eliezer of circumcision.
gershom:a7.1: No fewer than twenty-one blasts in the Temple, and no more than forty-eight: this is explained in tractate Sukkah, in the chapter HeḤalil.
rashi:a3.1: From two lyres: for two Levites.
rashi:a3.2: And not more than six: no reason is given.
tosafot:a3.1: (This belongs to the mishna.) And not more than six: Rashi explained that no reason is given. No fewer than two flutes and no more than twelve: corresponding to the twelve days on which the flute plays.
rashi:a3.3: From two flutes: ḥalil (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:a3.4: And not more than twelve: if they wished, they would use twelve, corresponding to the twelve days on which the flute plays before the altar.
rashi:a3.5: Plays [makkeh, literally “strikes”]: for there were holes in the flute, and he would strike the hole with his finger to make the sound pleasant.
rashi:a3.6: At the slaughter of the first Paschal offering: on the fourteenth of Nisan, when they would read the Hallel in the Temple courtyard at the time of the slaughter, as we say in the chapter Tamid Nishḥat (Pesachim 64a).
rashi:a3.7: Abuv: that is a ḥalil, and the Gemara explains it so.
rashi:a3.8: And one would conclude [meḥalek] only with a single flute: when they reached the end of the melody, one of the flutes would draw out its sound after the other fell silent, for that is a more beautiful ending than if both ended together. Ḥilluk means the ending, which divides one melody from the next. This music was played at the time of the offering: on those twelve days the Levites would sing the Hallel with their mouths while the flutes played. On the other days there were lyres, a cymbal and harps, and the song was the one set out in Rosh HaShana (31a): on the first day of the week, “The earth is the Lord’s, and all that it holds,” the whole psalm; on the second, “Great is the Lord and much acclaimed”; and so for all of them.
gershom:a8.1: No fewer than two lyres and no more than six: the reason for six is not explained to us. [Two lyres and no fewer, for so it says in the latter clause of our chapter: “and two lyres and a cymbal.”]
gershom:a9.1: Nevel [lyre]: a round wooden frame like a sieve, over which is stretched, on this side [and that], the stomach of the lamb [of the daily offering], as we learned in tractate (Tamid) [Kinnim]: “its innards for lyres,” that is the stomach; “its intestines for harps,” that is the thin ones. He would leave it to dry, and afterward strike the stomach, and it would make a great sound.
gershom:a13.1: And some say: a nevel is a harpa [a harp] in the vernacular.
gershom:a10.1: Two flutes: the reason for two is not explained to us.
gershom:a11.1: And no more than twelve: corresponding to the twelve (priests) [Levites] who stand on the platform, as is said below.
gershom:a12.1: Ḥalil: pipa [a pipe, in the vernacular].
gershom:a21.1: The flute plays [makkeh]: it plays forcefully before the altar.
gershom:a23.1: And one would conclude only with a single flute: that is, at the end of [this] song he would draw out the sound of the abuv longer than the other kinds of music, and with it he would end the song, because its sound is pleasant and it concludes and ends well.
rashi:a4.1: And they were slaves of priests: those who played the flute.
gershom:a24.1: And they were slaves of priests: from the other nations; those who played the musical instruments.
rashi:a4.2: Beit HaPegarim and Beit Tzippara: the names of the families.
rashi:a4.3: From Emaum: the name of the place.
rashi:a4.4: And they would marry into the priesthood: priests would marry their daughters, for they were Israelites of established lineage.
tosafot:a4.1: Some texts read Beit HaPegaris, with a samekh, and some read Beit HaPegarim, with a mem; and so it is written in the Tosefta (chapter 1), and the verse (Jeremiah 31) has “the valley of the corpses [pegarim].”
gershom:a25.1: And Rabbi Yosei says: they were Israelites of established lineage, from the family of the house of Pegaris and Tzippara.
gershom:a26.1: And they were from Emaum: from that place.
rashi:a5.1: Gemara. The mishna, which counts twenty-one blasts and forty-eight blasts, is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: for our mishna counts each tekia and each terua by itself, and there is no terua without a plain blast before it and after it; while Rabbi Yehuda counts a tekia, a terua and a tekia as only one. So you have: the twenty-one of our tanna are seven for Rabbi Yehuda, and the forty-eight of our tanna are sixteen for Rabbi Yehuda.
tosafot:a5.1: One may not sound fewer than seven: for Rabbi Yehuda, who says there are only seven blasts, since he counts tekia-terua-tekia as one blast. And as for what it says in Shabbat, in the chapter Bameh Madlikin (35b), that they would sound six blasts on Shabbat eve to stop the people from work: according to Rabbi Yehuda, who counts tekia-terua-tekia as one blast, those are only two. Rather, it said six according to the Rabbis, and we count tekia-terua-tekia as three blasts.
gershom:a14.1: He may not sound fewer than seven blasts each day, nor more than sixteen: that is, a third of what we learned in our mishna. Rabbi Yehuda holds that a tekia, a terua and a tekia are one; therefore he says seven, which are the twenty-one of our mishna, which counts each one by itself; and the sixteen of Rabbi Yehuda are the forty-eight of the mishna.
rashi:a7.1: And you shall sound [utkatem] a terua: evidently it calls a terua a tekia, and a tekia a terua.
gershom:a15.1: And you shall sound a terua: it calls a terua a tekia, and it calls a tekia a terua, as it is written “a terua they shall sound”; conclude from this that it is one.
rashi:a7.2: For a plain blast before it and after it: for from here we derive a plain blast before it, as it is written “and you shall sound [utkatem]” and then “terua,” and a plain blast after it, as it is written (Numbers 10:6) “terua” and then “they shall sound [yitke’u].” And in fact each one is a mitzva by itself.
rashi:a8.1: Merely a signal: a sign that they should assemble, and not for any mitzva.
gershom:a16.1: And Rabbi Yehuda: that “you shall sound a tekia and not a terua” is merely a signal to assemble; therefore one blast suffices. But for a mitzva [and the service, he counts] a tekia, a terua and a tekia as one.
rashi:a9.1: And not at all: that he should not delay and pause between the plain blast before and the terua, or between the terua and the plain blast after it; rather, all at once, close to one another.
tosafot:a9.1: There is no pause between a tekia and a terua at all: the Gemara concludes that this follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says tekia-terua-tekia is a single blast; and so too according to the Rabbis it is forbidden to pause between the blasts. From here it seemed to Rabbi [a Tosafist; the name is abbreviated] that it is forbidden to pause between the shevarim and the [terua]: for we are unsure whether [the terua is] groaning or wailing together, and so, out of doubt, we sound shevarim and terua together as one blast, and it is forbidden to pause between them. And if he was prevented during the terua and could not complete it, because of shortness of breath or some other constraint, he goes back to the shevarim; and Rabbi [likewise abbreviated] agreed with him. From here it is implied that it is forbidden to pause between one blast and the next. As for what we say in Shabbat (35b), that they would pause, where we say the first blast was to stop the people in the fields, the second to stop the city and its shops, and so on: there it is different, for since they instituted them so that each one is a sign for a different matter, it is not counted as a pause.
gershom:a17.1: There is no pause between a tekia and a terua at all: since it is one, he pauses nothing between them.
rashi:a9.2: In accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: who says they are a single mitzva and need no pause.
rashi:a10.1: Even in accordance with the Rabbis: and this “no pause between” would not mean that they must be so close together, only that he should not wait too long in between.
gershom:a18.1: Even the Rabbis: [lest you say that] this “not at all” is not precise, and it is said only to exclude Rabbi Yoḥanan, meaning he should not pause that long, though he may pause a little, in accordance with the Rabbis, who say they are two. [The Gemara] teaches us that he does not pause at all, in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
rashi:a10.2: And to exclude Rabbi Yoḥanan: who says regarding Rosh HaShana that if one heard nine blasts, three for Malkhuyot, three for Zikhronot and three for Shofarot, in nine hours, waiting an hour between each one, he has fulfilled his obligation.
gershom:a19.1: And say it is indeed so: that it can be established in accordance with the Rabbis.
rashi:a11.1: And not at all: this implies he should not pause at all.
gershom:a20.1: If so, what is “not at all”? This implies that he does not pause at all; evidently, because they are one.
gershom:a27.1: Since the individual completes the Hallel on them: at the slaughter of the Paschal offering one completes the Hallel. [A printed gloss adds that it should read: “but on the other days of Passover one does not complete it.”]
gershom:a28.1: [The printed text has here, in parentheses: “and on the two days of the slaughter of the Paschal offering one does not complete the Hallel.”] As we say there in tractate Pesachim: “they had not yet reached ‘I love’ [Psalms 116] because…”; evidently one completes the Hallel on them.
rashi:a13.1: The eight days of Hanukkah: the mishna does not count them, because there is no offering on them.
tosafot:a13.1: Eighteen days: the reason it does not count the eve of Passover, which would make nineteen, is that [that Hallel] is only in the Temple; so it does not count it.
tosafot:a13.2: In brief: Eighteen days on which the individual completes the Hallel: that is, on other days it is not said at all. One cannot explain that on other days one does not complete it but reads it with skipping, since the Gemara says “the New Moon is called an appointed day; let us say it,” implying that on the New Moon it is not said at all; likewise “what is different about the Festival, that we say it, and Passover, that we do not say it” implies there is no obligation at all on the New Moon or on [the rest of] Passover. So too in Ta’anit (28b): Rav came to Babylonia, saw them reciting Hallel on the New Moon and thought to stop them; when he saw they were skipping, he said, “They hold to the custom of their fathers.” This implies Rav thought it is not said at all, so what we say is only a custom, not an obligation as on the eighteen days. Even so, Rabbeinu Tam says one must bless over it: Rav thought to stop them, which implies they were blessing (otherwise, seeing no blessing, he would have understood at once that it was only custom); and in Berakhot (14b) Rava rules that on the eighteen days one may pause between sections but not in the middle of a section, while on days when the individual does not complete it one may pause even in the middle; if no blessing were said, what pause would matter? And then he could pause even for a voluntary matter, yet the question there was only about pausing out of fear or out of respect. This is unlike Sukkah (44b), “over a custom we do not bless”: that refers to a custom of handling, like the willow, but over a reading that is a custom one does bless. As for Ta’anit (28b), “an individual should not begin, but if he began he completes it”: it means an individual need not begin, and if he began he completes it, with skipping; this implies the community is obligated, out of custom. A small difficulty: how could Rav think to stop them, when it is taught there that the community must read it and an individual too completes it once he has begun? Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained: an individual should not begin with a blessing, but if he began with a blessing he completes it. In any case, hold to the view of Rabbeinu Tam that it is good for an individual too to bless at the start: although he is certainly not obligated to say it, since he takes it upon himself it is not a blessing in vain, just as women bless over taking the lulav and it is not in vain, since although they are exempt they may take it. rashi:b1.1: The days of the Festival are distinct in their offerings: for the bulls of the Festival keep decreasing.
gershom:b1.1: [Their offerings are distinct: the bulls of the Festival.]
gershom:b2.1: Shabbat, whose offerings are distinct from the other days of the week: let us say Hallel.
rashi:b3.1: The New Moon is called an appointed day [mo’ed]: as it is written (Lamentations 1:15), “He proclaimed a mo’ed against me”; and in the fourth chapter of tractate Ta’anit (29a): Tammuz of that year was made full, as it is written, “He proclaimed a mo’ed against me.”
gershom:b3.1: The New Moon, which is called an appointed day: let us complete the Hallel on it. See the Gemara in tractate Shevuot (10a): “He proclaimed a mo’ed against me”: Tammuz of that year was made full.
rashi:b3.3: Sanctified: with regard to the performance of labor.
tosafot:b5.1: The ministering angels said: Why do the Jewish people not recite song before You on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur? It does not say “Why do we not recite song,” which implies that the ministering angels do recite song. Therefore Ri says that on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur one should not skip [the line of the liturgy] “And the ḥayyot sing, and the cherubim glorify.”
gershom:b5.1: Which has neither this nor that: it is neither distinct in its offering, nor sanctified as a festival and forbidden in labor.
rashi:b8.1: Its reading: the reading of the Megilla.
gershom:b6.1: They returned to their initial permission: to recite song even outside the Land [by the reading of the Megilla].
rashi:b10.1: That its sound is sweet [ḥali]: its sound is sweet to hear.
rashi:b11.2: Thin: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss); its bark was thin.
rashi:b11.3: Cymbal [tziltzal]: two instruments struck one against the other, whose sound is thin; they are called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
gershom:b7.1: Tziltzul [cymbal]: they call them tzimbash [tzibli] (a vernacular gloss), and they are like [two] copper discs that are struck against each other.
rashi:b12.1: It would compound the spices: in it they would pound the ingredients of the incense; its sound was clear, and it compounded the spices well and gave them fragrance, as we say in Keritot (6b): the one who grinds says, “Grind thoroughly, thoroughly grind,” because the voice is good for the spices.
gershom:b8.1: It would compound the spices: it gave the spices a good fragrance.
rashi:b13.1: Two vessels: the cymbal and the copper mortar.
rashi:b13.2: Burnished [memorat]: thin, so that one can fold it.
rashi:b13.3: Bright [memorak]: polished (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
tosafot:b12.1: And concerning them David said, “burnished brass”: Rashi explained it as about the brass [the rest of his phrase here is unclear]. But it is difficult: this verse is simply in Kings, where “burnished brass” is written, and in Chronicles (II 4) “bright brass” is written; so what does “and concerning them David said” mean? It seems to Ri that the reading is: “and concerning them the verse says, burnished brass, (bright) brass.”
gershom:b9.1: They were remnants from the First Temple: from the Tabernacle.
gershom:b11.1: Bright [memorak]: very smooth. And they still existed in the days of Ezra, and concerning them it says, and so on.
rashi:b15.1: Pairs: two cymbals and two mortars.
gershom:b12.1: [They were pairs: two mortars and two cymbals.]
rashi:b16.1: Like an issar: the mouth of the spring, where it gushes out, was as wide as an issar.
rashi:b16.2: Let not the wise man glory: for his wisdom only spoils, since the vessels of the First Temple were made by the word of the Almighty, as it is written (I Chronicles 28[:19]): “All this in writing, from the hand of the Lord upon me; He made me understand all the work of the pattern.”
tosafot:b17.1: Rashi reads hirdavlis, with a samekh, and it seems to Rabbi [a Tosafist] that it is hirdavlim, with a mem; and so in Bereshit Rabba: “ardavlin in the city, and the province was overturned”; ardavlin is like hirdavlin, and they are kinds of musical instruments, as mem interchanges with nun. Hirdavlim is the Aramaic translation of ugav [an organ].
rashi:b17.1: Hirdavlis, tavla gurgedana [Rashi’s reading; see Tosafot]: a bell and its clapper, which they call (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b17.2: And it disrupts the melody: when this sound was ending.
gershom:b14.1: Gudgena [so Rabbeinu Gershom reads]: kloguta (with a vernacular gloss), [of that kind].
gershom:b15.1: And it disrupts the melody: of the song.
rashi:b18.1: Magreifa: with which they rake up the ashes of the altar (Rashi adds an Old French gloss); it is like a scoop.
tosafot:b18.1: There was a magreifa in the Temple: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained it as the one with which they rake up the ashes. But it is difficult, since this one was a musical instrument! Rather, it seems one should explain that there were two kinds of magreifa: one for the ashes and one for song.
gershom:b16.1: Magreifa: a vessel with which they rake the ashes from the altar.
